Customer Portal Builders: How to Choose and Launch One Fast (May 2026)
summary: Learn how to choose customer portal builders and launch fast in May 2026. Compare features, security, and implementation timelines for your business needs.
body_text: Everyone says they want a customer portal, but most teams stall because they're not sure which customer portal builder to use or how long it'll take to get live. The good news: if you already have your data in a spreadsheet, CRM, or database, you can connect a home builder customer portal or any business portal in a week or two. You just need to know what to focus on so you don't overbuild or pick a tool that doesn't fit your permission model. TLDR: Portal builders cut support volume by giving customers self-service access to orders and files. Role-based permissions, two-way data sync, and SSO support are non-negotiable features. Portal builders launch in days to weeks; custom development takes months and needs engineers. Most portal failures come from skipping permissions setup or launching without user testing. Stacker connects to your existing data sources and builds portals through AI-assisted conversation. What Is a Customer Portal Builder A customer portal builder is a tool that lets you create a private, web-based workspace where your customers can log in, view their data, submit requests, track orders, or manage their accounts without you writing a single line of code. Learn more about customer portals and how they work. Unlike general website builders, these tools are built around access control and data. You decide who sees what, connect the portal to your existing records, and give each customer a personalized view of only their information. Home builders, service firms, and SaaS companies all use them to reduce repetitive status emails and support requests. Benefits of Building a Customer Portal A customer portal gives clients instant self-service access and frees your team from having to field the same status questions repeatedly. The gains show up across several areas: Self-service access reduces inbound support volume by letting customers look up contracts, project updates, or billing records on demand without emailing your team. Shared visibility reduces back-and-forth by giving customers and your team a single source of truth for files, statuses, and next steps. Role-based permissions let you control exactly what each customer sees, so sensitive data stays protected without requiring manual gatekeeping. A branded customer portal experience builds trust, especially for home builder customer portal use cases where homeowners track construction milestones and warranty details over months or years. For home builders and contractors, this last point carries extra weight. A homeowner portal keeps buyers informed through every phase of a build, reducing anxious check-in calls and building confidence in your process before the keys are handed over. Key Features to Look for in a Portal Builder Not all portal builders handle the same workload. Some manage simple read-only views without issue, but break down once you add multiple user types, live data connections, or a branded experience that looks like your business. Here are the features worth checking before you commit: Role-based permissions: controls who can see which records or fields, and are table stakes for any portal serving more than one type of user Authentication: secure, low-friction login out of the box, with SSO support for teams that need it Data integration: two-way sync with the tools you already run on, so records stay in one place Workflow automation: status updates, approvals, and notifications that trigger on their own without manual follow-up Mobile responsiveness: works cleanly on any device without a separate build Branding controls: custom colors, fonts, and layouts tied to your business, not the tool's defaults Security and Compliance Requirements When you give external users access to your data, security becomes mandatory. A customer portal builder needs to support role-based permissions so that each user sees only what they're supposed to. Look for SSO support, audit logs, and encryption both in transit and at rest. If your business handles sensitive information, check whether the builder meets relevant compliance standards. Here is what each standard means in practice: SOC 2 Type II: Confirms the vendor has been independently audited on security, availability, and confidentiality controls over a period of time (typically six to twelve months). A Type II report is stronger evidence than a Type I, which only covers a single point in time. Ask vendors for their most recent report and check when it was issued. GDPR: Applies if any of your portal users are based in the EU or if you process data of EU residents. Check where the vendor stores data, whether they offer a Data Processing Agreement (DPA), and whether they support data deletion requests. Storing data on EU-based servers significantly simplifies compliance. HIPAA: Required if your portal handles protected health information (PHI). Look for a vendor willing to sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), which is required under HIPAA. Not all portal builders offer this, and those that do typically reserve it for higher-tier plans. Some builders offer these certifications out of the box; others require a higher-tier plan or custom configuration. Confirm which tier includes the compliance features you need before signing a contract. Upgrading later can be disruptive and costly. Questions to Ask Before You Commit Does the builder support row-level or field-level permissions, so you can restrict access at a granular level within a single view? Is SSO available on your target plan, or is it gated behind an enterprise tier? Where is customer data stored, and in which region? This matters if you operate in the EU or handle sensitive or compliance-governed data. Does the vendor publish a SOC 2 Type II report or similar third-party audit that you can share with your own compliance team? Skipping this checklist early is a common mistake. Rebuilding a portal after a security gap surfaces costs far more time than vetting requirements upfront. Data Integration and Backend Connectivity A customer portal is only as useful as the data it can read and write. If your portal sits disconnected from your CRM, project management tool, or billing system, your team ends up doing double-entry work, and your clients get stale information. Look for a builder that connects directly to the sources you already rely on. The best options support two-way sync, so changes made in the portal are automatically reflected in your source data. Common integrations worth confirming before you commit: CRM connections (Salesforce, HubSpot) so client records stay current without manual exports Spreadsheet sync (Google Sheets, Airtable) for teams whose data still lives in rows and columns Database support (PostgreSQL, MySQL) for businesses with structured backend data REST API access for connecting to custom or less common data sources DIY Portal Builders vs Custom Development There are two paths to building a customer portal: hire developers to build one from scratch, or use a dedicated customer portal builder. Custom development gives you full control, but that control comes at a cost. Projects routinely take months and require ongoing engineering resources just to maintain what you've built. Portal builders sit in the middle ground. You get a configurable product without the dev overhead, and most teams can go from setup to launch in days instead of quarters. Custom builds suit companies with highly specialized workflows that no off-the-shelf tool can handle, and a dedicated engineering team to support them long-term. Portal builders work well for ops teams, client success managers, and small-to-mid-size businesses that need something real up and running fast, without waiting in a dev queue. Factor Custom Development Portal Builder Time to launch Months Days to weeks Upfront cost High Low to moderate Maintenance burden High (engineering required) Low (managed by vendor) Flexibility Unlimited Configurable within the tool Best for Unique, complex workflows Standard portal use cases The trade-off is honest: custom code scales to nearly any requirement, but most businesses never need to reach that ceiling. A well-chosen portal builder covers use cases like client onboarding, order tracking, document access, and project status views faster and more cheaply. How to Choose the Right Portal Builder for Your Business Before committing to a builder , it helps to run through a short checklist of questions that will quickly narrow your options. Here are the factors worth weighing: What data source are you connecting to? If your business already runs on Google Sheets, Airtable, or a SQL database, look for a builder that connects directly to those sources instead of forcing a migration. Who are your portal users? External clients need stricter permission controls than internal staff. Confirm that the builder supports row-level or role-based access before you proceed. How much customization do you need? Some builders offer ready-made templates that get you live in hours; others give you more layout control but take longer to configure. What does your team look like? If no one on your team writes code, rule out any builder that requires it for basic setup or ongoing changes. What is your budget? Pricing models vary widely, from per-user fees to flat monthly tiers, so map the cost against your expected number of portal users. A Note on Home Builder Customer Portals Home builders and residential contractors have specific requirements that not every builder handles well. You need clients to track build progress, approve selections, and access documents, all without having to call your office. Look for a builder that supports file uploads, status tracking views, and conditional visibility so buyers only see what applies to their lot or phase. The right choice comes down to fit: match the builder's strengths to your actual workflow, not the one with the longest feature list. Implementation Timeline and Launch Strategy Most customer portal projects stall not because of the tech, but because teams underestimate the sequencing. A clear launch order keeps you moving. A Realistic Four-Week Timeline Here is a sequencing that works for most teams building with a no-code customer portal builder: Week 1: Define your use case and data structure . Identify which data sources the portal needs to read from or write to, and map out which user roles need access to what. Week 2: Build your first working view. Connect your data source, set up role-based permissions, and get one core workflow functional before adding more. Week 3: Test with five to ten actual customers or team members, collect feedback, and fix the friction points you find. Week 4: Fix, refine, and open access. Resolve the issues from testing, finalize your branding, and roll out to your full user base. What to Tackle Before You Build Jumping into a build before you have clarity on a few questions tends to create rework. Before touching any tool, confirm: Who your external users are and what they need to do inside the portal Where your data currently lives and whether it can connect via API or native integration What your permission structure looks like across different customer tiers or roles Whether you need two-way data sync or read-only access Getting these answered in writing, even briefly, cuts build time considerably. Measuring Portal Success and ROI After your portal goes live, tracking a few key numbers tells you whether it's actually working or just adding complexity. Adoption rate: What share of eligible users logged in during the first 30 days? A healthy portal typically sees 60–80% of invited users log in within the first month. Low adoption usually points to onboarding friction, a confusing invite email, an unclear login flow, or a homepage that doesn't surface the right information immediately. Fix the entry experience before assuming users don't need the portal. Support ticket volume: A well-built portal should reduce the need for clients or vendors to ask repetitive status questions. Measure ticket volume in the 30 days before launch and compare it to the 30 days after. If volume hasn't dropped by the 60-day mark, audit which self-service features are going unused and whether the data behind them is current and accurate. Time-to-resolution: Track how long it takes from a client submitting a request to receiving a response or resolution. Portals with two-way sync and automated notifications tend to cut resolution time by removing the back-and-forth of email chains. If resolution times aren't improving, check whether notifications are firing correctly and whether clients can actually find the request submission flow. Data accuracy rate: If clients are emailing to flag wrong information in the portal, your data sync has a gap. Track how often clients report stale or incorrect records. Even one or two complaints per week erodes trust quickly. Set up a simple log to capture these reports and trace them back to the source. Review these four numbers together at the 30, 60, and 90-day marks. A portal that scores well on adoption but poorly on ticket reduction likely has a feature discoverability problem, not a data problem. Common Portal Implementation Mistakes Skipping permissions setup is one of the most common ways a portal launch goes sideways. If every user can see every record, you'll get support tickets from confused clients and, worse, potential data exposure. Map out your user roles before you write a single line of configuration. The second mistake is building without real user input. A portal that looks complete internally can still confuse the people it was built for. Run a quick walkthrough with two or three actual clients before you go live. Finally, watch for data sync gaps. If your portal pulls from a spreadsheet or database that teams update manually, outdated information erodes trust fast. Confirm your data source is live and accurate before launch day. Building a Customer Portal With Stacker Stacker is an AI-powered app-building tool built around portal use cases. Teams across industries run critical workflows on Stacker, from client onboarding and document management to application review systems. Where horizontal AI tools require you to explain what a good portal looks like from scratch, Stacker already knows. Years of portal-specific use cases are baked into the AI, so the output is production-ready. As your requirements change, you refine through conversation instead of filing a ticket and waiting. Final Thoughts on Selecting the Right Portal Builder Most teams don't need unlimited customization; they need a working portal that handles their actual use case without months of development time. The right customer portal builder integrates with the tools you already use, protects sensitive data with role-based permissions, and gives your clients self-service access that reduces support volume. If your business runs on spreadsheets, CRMs, or databases and you need external users to securely view their records, book a demo to see how Stacker handles portal builds. FAQ Can I build a customer portal without coding? Yes. Modern portal builders like Stacker let you create fully functional client portals by describing what you need in plain language, no code required. The AI handles authentication, permissions, and data connections while you focus on which information your customers need to access. Customer portal builder vs custom development? Portal builders launch in days with low upfront cost and managed maintenance, while custom development takes months, costs far more, and requires ongoing engineering resources. Custom builds suit highly specialized workflows with dedicated dev teams; portal builders fit standard use cases where speed and cost matter more than unlimited flexibility. What's the difference between a customer portal and a regular website builder? A customer portal builder is built around access control and personalized data views, where each customer logs in and sees only their information. How long does it take to launch a customer portal? Most teams go from setup to launch in two to four weeks when using a no-code portal builder. Week one covers data structure and use-case definition; week two builds the first working view; week three runs user testing; and week four handles refinements before the full rollout. What security features should a home builder's customer portal include? Role-based permissions so each homeowner sees only their project data, secure authentication with SSO support, audit logs tracking who accessed what, and encryption for data in transit and at rest. If you handle sensitive financial or personal information, verify the builder meets SOC 2 or relevant compliance standards before committing.

title: Illinois American Water Announces Upcoming Hydrant Flushing in Lincoln
summary: Annual Flushing starts Tuesday, July 28 and continues through August 21 LINCOLN, Ill. (July 27, 2026) – Beginning tomorrow, Illinois American Water’s Lincoln District will perform flushing of...
body_text: Annual Flushing starts Tuesday, July 28 and continues through August 21 LINCOLN, Ill. (July 27, 2026) – Beginning tomorrow, Illinois American Water’s Lincoln District will perform flushing of its water distribution system to continue to provide customers with high-quality, reliable water service in Lincoln. This work will occur between 7 AM and 3 PM during weekdays and should be completed by August 21, 2026. “Scheduled annually to maintain and improve water service, flushing removes mineral deposits and sediment from water mains, helping us to continue to provide our customers with high-quality water service,” said Amanda Scott, Manager of Operations, Illinois American Water . “This planned work for our water distribution systems is an essential part of Illinois American Water’s maintenance program, which also allows us to inspect our fire hydrants to confirm they are operational and to check fire flows in the system.” Flushing involves simultaneously opening fire hydrants in a specific area to create increased water flows. This routine flushing program also includes flushing blowoff valves on dead-end water mains throughout the system. Tips for Customers During Flushing Season While water mains are being cleaned, no interruptions in water service are expected, but customers may notice short periods of low water pressure or discolored water. During the flushing process, the following steps are encouraged: Store a large pitcher of water in the refrigerator for drinking. Check for discolored water before using the washing machine or dishwasher. After flushing is complete: If temporary water discoloration occurs, run cold water until it is clear. If water pressure or water volume seems low, check and clean faucet aerators. For more flushing information and tips to prepare, visit https://newsroom.amwater.com/PrepareForFlushing . Scott adds, “When Illinois American Water crews are flushing a hydrant, the general public is asked to stay away from the area for their safety and to give our employees enough space to complete their work.” Illinois American Water notifies customers when flushing is scheduled to take place in their area through its mass notification system and asks customers to take a few moments to update their contact information and preferences in their MyWater account. Customers must opt-in for general alerts to receive local flushing and other non-emergency notifications via phone call, text or email. Individuals who are not Illinois American Water account holders can check the Alerts webpage and Customer Advisory Map on the company’s website for the latest updates regarding any potential service disruptions due to planned work or emergencies. About American Water American Water (NYSE: AWK) is the largest regulated water and wastewater utility company in the United States. With a history dating back to 1886 and celebrating 140 years in 2026, We Keep Life Flowing® by providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable drinking water and wastewater services to approximately 14 million people with regulated operations in 14 states and on 18 military installations. American Water’s approximately 7,000 talented professionals leverage their significant expertise and the company’s national size and scale to achieve excellent outcomes for the benefit of customers, employees, investors and other stakeholders. For more information, visit amwater.com and join American Water on LinkedIn , Facebook , X, and Instagram . About Illinois American Water Illinois American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, is the largest regulated water utility in the state with approximately 600 dedicated employees working to provide safe, clean, reliable and affordable water and wastewater services to approximately 1.3 million people. American Water also operates a quality control and research laboratory in Belleville. Media Contact: Anna Kubas External Communications Illinois American Water Anna.Kubas@amwater.com

title: 「精彩時刻」：在 Roblox 上探索下一款最愛遊戲的更多方式
summary: Roblox 推出全新首頁，新增「時刻」、「聊天」及「我的專頁」分頁
body_text: 分享 新聞 產品 「精彩時刻」：在 Roblox 上探索下一款最愛遊戲的更多方式 Roblox 應用程式現已整合聊天、遊玩、探索與創作功能於一處 發佈者 塞布·巴里奧斯，工程部門資深副總裁 發佈日期 2026年7月28日 從今天起，在加拿大、紐西蘭和新加坡開啟 Roblox 的玩家將開始看到全新的應用程式首頁，其中包含「Moments」、「聊天」和「我」這三個分頁（紐西蘭的玩家還會看到 「建造」 分頁）。這些分頁將在未來幾個月內逐步在全球*推出。 「時刻」是一種探索遊戲的新方式：玩家可以觀看朋友和影片內容創作者的遊戲片段，並透過輕觸一下即可加入有趣的遊戲。每個「時刻」都是通往遊戲的入口。 「聊天」功能讓玩家能進行一場連續的對話，並能無縫地將對話帶入遊戲中——無需離開 Roblox。 「我」將虛擬角色與個人檔案整合於一處，讓玩家更輕鬆地展現自我。 從今天起，加拿大、紐西蘭和新加坡的玩家將開始看到全新版 Roblox 應用程式，其中包含「Moments」、「Chat」和「Me」三個分頁。這些分頁將在未來數月內全球*逐步推出。對於紐西蘭的玩家來說，全新的 「Build」 分頁——這是 Roblox Studio 的延伸功能，可在應用程式內提供以行動裝置為優先的創作體驗——也將從今天起陸續出現。 每天平均有 1.32 億活躍用戶造訪 Roblox，體驗數百萬款可供遊玩的遊戲。而每天，我們的創作者社群都會推出更多值得嘗試的遊戲，從模擬遊戲和策略遊戲，到高保真、沉浸式的多人遊戲世界。透過將玩家與他們真正喜愛並會一再回訪的遊戲進行配對，我們協助創作者拓展事業，並找到最熱衷的受眾群體。 在 Roblox 平台之外，人們可能在某些地方與朋友聊天或分享遊戲，但朋友必須點擊三次並安裝應用程式才能開始遊玩。我們希望玩家能夠在同一個地方推薦、探索和尋找遊戲，無需額外步驟。因此，我們正在擴展 Roblox 應用程式，以支援完整的流程——在同一個地方與朋友聊天、查看其他人正在玩什麼，並直接點擊進入精彩的遊戲。 今年稍早，我們針對玩家會持續遊玩的遊戲， 優化了 遊戲探索與推薦系統，並透過 Roblox 首頁的「為您推薦」專區，向玩家展示相關遊戲。當 「Moments」 最初以測試版推出時，我們將其視為遊戲探索的額外引擎。 如今，「Moments」已成為 Roblox 上的專屬分頁*。透過玩家與影片創作者提供的多元內容，「Moments」打造出無縫的體驗，讓您只需輕點一下，即可瀏覽並遊玩遊戲。 Moments：立即探索並遊玩新遊戲 「Moments」的設計初衷，是為精彩遊戲與熱愛它的玩家之間架設一條直通之路。年滿 16 歲* 且通過年齡驗證的玩家，可以瀏覽朋友和其他玩家分享的遊戲實況影片，並只需輕點一下即可親自體驗遊戲。 「Moments」分頁的全新亮點，是精選內容創作者製作的高品質 Roblox 內容影片，類似於玩家在其他平台所見到的這些創作者分享的內容。但在「Moments」中，這些影片不僅分享遊戲精華片段，更直接連結至影片中介紹的遊戲，讓玩家只需輕點一下即可開始遊玩。與我們其他 發現系統 一樣，「Moments」經過優化，旨在讓玩家與他們會喜愛並願意回訪的遊戲建立連結。 在「Moments」分頁中，每則貼文都是通往遊戲的入口。玩家只需點擊每個遊戲片段下方的「加入」按鈕，即可立即開始遊玩。這正是發現精彩新遊戲的捷徑。 聊天：跨遊戲連線與遊玩 「聊天」是玩家向朋友推薦遊戲、協調遊戲時段，甚至一起加入遊戲的地方。這點至關重要，因為人們回歸並非僅為了玩遊戲，而是為了與朋友建立連結並一同遊玩。當朋友說：「嘿，你一定要試試這款遊戲」時，我們希望加入該遊戲的過程能盡可能簡單。 從今天起，所有符合聊天資格的玩家都將看到「聊天」分頁。不久之後，我們將實現跨遊戲對話功能，讓朋友們在遊玩時能無縫保持聯繫，無需切換應用程式或在不同裝置間協調。 「 聊天」 功能建基於 年齡驗證 、 Roblox Kids 及 Select 帳戶等基礎功能之上，僅在符合玩家 年齡適宜性 時才會啟用。透過 「可信朋友 」功能與 即時聊天內容重述機制 ，我們讓各年齡層的玩家都能更輕鬆地建立連結——同時提供各項保護措施，確保他們的安全。 我：自我表達，一鍵搞定 「頭像」分頁現已更名為「我的資料」分頁，讓玩家能輕鬆地在同一個頁面更新個人資料及頭像外觀。在此，玩家可從數種新的頭像背景中進行選擇，為自我表達增添更多可能性。 Build：拓展 Roblox 的無限可能 我們 全新的應用程式內創作功能 「Build」分頁的公開測試版，將於今日開始向紐西蘭境內年滿 9 歲且已通過年齡驗證的用戶逐步推出。「Build」是一款以行動裝置為優先的遊戲創作體驗，旨在與「Studio」協同運作，並共用相同的後端系統、模型及聊天紀錄。 從今天起，參與公開測試的創作者可以在手機上透過「Build」開始製作遊戲，然後利用「Studio」更廣泛的功能來精修作品。一旦該分頁正式上線，他們還將能夠在「Studio」中開始製作，並透過行動裝置查看進度。透過「Build」，我們不僅擴展了 Roblox 支援的遊戲類型，也擴大了能夠創作這些遊戲的群體。 這標誌著 Roblox 玩家嶄新篇章的開端——一個能與朋友聯繫、探索朋友和喜愛的影音內容創作者正在遊玩什麼、展現自我，甚至可能打造出完全嶄新事物的統一平台。我們迫不及待想見證社群將如何運用這項功能。 *可用性與功能將因年齡及地區而異。

title: Advano establishes New Orleans, Louisiana operations
summary: Advano established silicon battery materials operations at the New Orleans Regional Business Park in New Orleans, Louisiana.
body_text: Advano established silicon battery materials operations at the New Orleans Regional Business Park in New Orleans, Louisiana. The project is expected to create up to 25 jobs. The new pilot plant will deliver ton-scale volumes of the company’s proprietary technology, REALSi, and enter electric vehicle qualification programs in 2024. REALSi are drop-in technologies providing cost-effective, high-performing solutions for current lithium-ion batteries across various sectors, including electric vehicles, consumer electronics, and defense. “The key challenge in today’s batteries is safe energy density enhancement. At Advano, our proprietary silicon technologies tackle this challenge by providing cost-effective, regionally produced solutions to boost energy density in next generation batteries,” said Chris York, CEO of Advano. “The integration of our critical materials enhances EV consumers’ ability to qualify for substantial tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act. This enables a clear path for cost-effective transitioning to EVs and assisting consumer choice to address climate change.” Advano has developed a next-generation silicon technology for Lithium-ion batteries. The company utilizes earth-abundant raw materials and a sustainable and scalable manufacturing process to create high-performance silicon anode materials. “Advano’s Specialty Pilot Plant in New Orleans East is a great win for the region that aligns with and advances our all-of-the-above energy strategy” noted Michael Hecht, President and CEO of Greater New Orleans, Inc. “This project is a great example of developing a clean energy solution while also creating jobs and investment in our communities. We see this project as a testament to the strength of the business infrastructure and assets in the region and state that can support companies like Advano from the lab to reality. GNO, Inc. looks forward to continuing our partnership with Advano and supporting their growth in New Orleans East.” “Advano is exactly the type of next-generation advanced manufacturing company we want to see continuing to invest in our city,” added Louis David, President and CEO of New Orleans Business Alliance. “New Orleans Business Alliance is proud to have worked with the company for years on site selection, talent connections and community involvement. Advano’s new pilot facility continues a long tradition of cutting-edge transportation technology being developed in New Orleans, from NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility right across the street to Advano’s electric vehicle battery innovations.” BACK TO TOP

title: Enphase Energy Highlights Safety and Reliability of the IQ EV Charger 2 Across Europe
summary: FREMONT, Calif., July 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enphase Energy, Inc. As home charging becomes increasingly important to EV owners, the
body_text: FREMONT, Calif., July 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: ENPH), a global energy technology company, today highlighted the safety and reliability of its IQ® EV Charger 2, now available across European markets. As home charging becomes increasingly important to EV owners, the IQ EV Charger 2 brings together robust thermal engineering, independent certifications, and built-in safety protections to deliver reliable performance across Europe’s varied climates. Many EV chargers reduce their output as temperatures rise, a behavior known as thermal derating that can slow charging on hot days or during long sessions. The IQ EV Charger 2 is engineered to reduce thermal derating across a broad range of operating conditions, helping homeowners get consistent charging performance year-round while maintaining safe operation. The IQ EV Charger 2 is engineered to operate across an ambient temperature range of –40°C to 55°C and at altitudes up to 2,500 meters. Its thermal design is built to sustain consistent charging output as temperatures rise, minimizing performance drop-off in hot conditions. Housed in a rugged IP55- and IK10-rated enclosure, the charger is weatherproof and impact-resistant for both indoor and outdoor installation. It supports single-phase and three-phase wiring with configurable power up to 32 A per phase and features automatic phase switching. Safety is engineered in from the hardware up. The IQ EV Charger 2 is safety certified by TÜV Rheinland, an independent testing organization, with energy-metering certification by NMI. The charger carries CE marking and complies with the applicable European standards for EV supply equipment, including IEC/EN 61851-1, IEC/EN 61851-21-2, IEC/EN 62196, and IEC/EN 62955, along with other market-specific certifications. In France, the charger has earned E.V. READY certification. It incorporates layered hardware protection, including overvoltage protection, overcurrent detection, an integrated residual direct current detecting device (RDC-DD), relay weld detection, and PEN fault detection, working together to help protect the vehicle, the home electrical system, and the user during charging. Beyond its hardware, the IQ EV Charger 2 works with Enphase solar and battery systems or as a standalone charger, offering dynamic load balancing, a certified Class B MID energy meter with +/- 1% accuracy for energy tracking, and smart charging that can prioritize surplus solar energy. Every IQ EV Charger 2 activated in supported European markets is backed by an industry-leading five-year warranty and 24/7 customer support from Enphase. "When we offer a charger, it has to perform reliably in the field, every day and in every season," said Jannik Schall, chief product officer and co-founder of 1KOMMA5°. "The IQ EV Charger 2 delivers the consistent performance and build quality our customers expect, with fewer surprises for them and for our installers." "Our customers trust the IQ EV Charger 2 to safely power one of their most important investments, their vehicle, every single day," said Sabbas Daniel, senior vice president of sales at Enphase Energy. "That trust is earned through rigorous engineering, independent certification, and layers of built-in protection, backed by an industry-leading five-year warranty and around-the-clock support. We designed it to be dependable for the long haul." The IQ EV Charger 2 is available across European markets in socketed and tethered configurations. The tethered configuration includes a rugged 7.5-meter charging cable with a Type 2 connector for installation flexibility. For more information about the IQ EV Charger 2, visit the applicable Enphase regional websites. Additional engineering and testing information is available in the IQ EV Charger 2 white paper . About Enphase Energy, Inc. Enphase Energy, a global energy technology company based in Fremont, CA, is the world's leading supplier of microinverter-based solar and battery systems, EV chargers, home energy management systems, and virtual power plant (VPP) solutions. Enphase products enable people to harness the sun to make, use, save, and sell their own power, all controlled through the Enphase App. The company revolutionized the solar industry with its microinverter-based technology and has shipped approximately 87.8 million microinverters, with more than 5.2 million Enphase-based systems deployed in over 165 countries. title: Headless architecture: What is it, and why is it the future?
summary: Learn about headless architecture and its basic principles. Discover the benefits of headless approach and decide if it’s the right fit for your business.
body_text: Headless architecture is a relatively new software development concept popular within industries that favor flexibility and scalability – like the ecommerce industry with the headless commerce approach. But how does it work, and in what way does it benefit online businesses? Why do companies want to become headless? In this article, you'll learn about the principles of headless architecture, why businesses are so keen on using it, and how to move from a monolith legacy solution and jump on the headless train. Keep reading to discover: What headless architecture is; The difference between headless architecture and microservices; The main benefits of headless architecture for ecommerce. Let’s dive in! What is headless architecture? Headless architecture is a software development concept where the frontend (user interface – UI) is separated from the backend (business logic) layer of the website. This decoupling allows for better customization, faster development, and a much quicker time-to-market for businesses. By offering unmatched technical flexibility, headless commerce empowers brands to craft a unique platform that aligns perfectly with business goals, integrates with your current tech stack, and delivers an exceptional customer experience. What is a headless commerce platform? When it comes to the ecommerce industry specifically, headless commerce is part of a bigger approach called composable commerce where ecommerce businesses can choose the ideal set of technologies along with the microservices they need, and combine them into a unique composition that fits their business requirements. A headless ecommerce solution is a decoupled system. Contrary to traditional ones, headless platforms separate the presentation layer from the commerce engine. Since it's API-based, the implementation is fast, and the system runs seamlessly. Headless architecture vs. microservices When researching the headless topic, many look for comparisons of headless commerce vs. microservices. It gets even more complicated as both terms occur in the MACH abbreviation, which stands for microservices-based, API-first, cloud-native, and headless. Does it mean they are the same? Well, not really. To avoid misunderstandings, let's clarify the difference. Headless architecture emphasizes decoupling the frontend and the backend layers of a system. This is, however, just one step towards composable architecture based on microservices. Microservices are small applications dedicated to a specific task. They can be easily replaced, independently developed, and installed, as a part of a larger software system composition. Microservices allow businesses to cherry-pick tech providers for each business function without having to modify the rest of the system. Headless vs. composable: What's the difference? While both headless and composable commerce share the goal of enhancing flexibility and customization in ecommerce, they operate at different levels of architectural design. Headless architecture specifically focuses on decoupling the frontend from the backend, enabling businesses to create tailored user experiences without being constrained by legacy systems. In contrast, composable commerce takes this a step further : it allows companies to integrate various best-of-breed solutions, including microservices, into a cohesive system. This means that with composable commerce, you can select and assemble the optimal technologies and services for each aspect of your business, creating a highly customized solution that aligns with what you need for your ecommerce platform. Essentially, while headless provides the foundational flexibility needed to innovate at the frontend side of things, composable commerce gives you a way to combine multiple services seamlessly, enhancing agility and responsiveness in a rapidly evolving market. How do they differ from monolithic architecture? Monolithic architecture is like a one-size-fits-all solution, where the frontend and backend components are tightly integrated into a single codebase. One great example of a well-known monolithic solution is SAP , where everything is built into one, unified system. While this approach may seem convenient, it often leads to challenges in scalability and adaptability. When you need to make updates or add new features, you’ll find that it requires a significant investment of time and resources, limiting your ability to respond to market changes or customer needs effectively. On the other hand, headless and composable architectures offer a refreshing alternative. Both decoupling the frontend and microservices integration allow for rapid customization and scalability, giving you the possibility to deliver engaging user experiences without the burden of being tied to a rigid structure. Benefits of headless architecture Headless architecture introduces a number of benefits to ecommerce businesses, offering distinct advantages over traditional, monolithic setups. Here are the most important ones: Separated presentation layer First and foremost, a headless solution gives you the flexibility to choose the best way to build your frontend layer . Thanks to this approach, you are no longer tied to the legacy frontend technology provided by your monolithic system. Omnichannel capabilities A headless commerce architecture helps to streamline the integration of content and product data, enabling customers to enjoy a consistent shopping experience across multiple channels. It opens up unlimited possibilities to approach omnichannel sales and frees marketing specialists to introduce changes to the website without the help of a developer team. Improved customer experience Frontend is where the entire customer journey happens; the ability to control the presentation layer of the system helps merchants to improve and personalize the customer experience of their online store. Coupled with fast web performance, it directly translates into increased conversions and higher revenue . Fast loading times Speaking of web performance, headless architecture focuses on delivering lightning-speed ecommerce websites . Since the frontend isn’t bound to a specific backend technology, it can leverage faster, modern frameworks like React or Vue that are built for speed. As the load times influence SEO results, the user experience, and conversion rates, it remains one of the most important benefits of headless commerce . Competitive edge An undeniable benefit of headless architecture is the agility and flexibility it gives to face an intensely competitive ecommerce market. Headless commerce enables rapid and flexible customization, allowing businesses to adapt quickly to market trends without overhauling the backend infrastructure. This not only streamlines the development process but also helps you to create engaging customer experiences that set your brand apart. Understanding headless CMS As we explore the components of headless architecture, it’s essential to understand how headless CMS plays a pivotal role in enabling flexible content delivery across diverse platforms. Headless Content Management Systems (CMS) are designed to separate the content creation and management process from the presentation layer, providing a more flexible and streamlined approach to content delivery. Unlike traditional CMS platforms that couple the frontend and backend tightly, a headless CMS focuses on content storage and management, delivering content through APIs to any front-end interface. This enables businesses to serve content across multiple channels seamlessly. How headless CMS works In a headless CMS, content is created, managed, and stored in the backend, while the frontend presentation layer is entirely decoupled; users access the headless CMS through an admin interface to create and manage content. This may include text, images, videos, and other digital assets. The CMS allows for easy categorization and structuring of content, which can be tailored to various use cases. Once the content is created, it is stored in a structured format within the CMS. The headless CMS then exposes this content via APIs that allow developers to request specific pieces of content and deliver them to any frontend application or device, ensuring that content can be accessed as needed. But that's not all there is to it: since it's headless, developers can build the frontend using their preferred technologies, such as modern JS frameworks. Because of the headless approach, developers are free to create custom user interfaces without being constrained by the backend architecture. Let's pinpoint the main differences between headless vs. traditional CMS : Traditional CMS consists of: Headless CMS has only: A database (where web content and digital assets are stored); An admin panel for managing content; A visual layer that presents information from the database using frontend technologies; A page rendering engine that brings these three elements together. A database for storing content; An API with access to HTTP queries; An admin panel Popular examples of headless CMS Several headless CMS platforms are making waves in the market, each with unique features and capabilities. Here are a few noteworthy examples: Contentful : A powerful and popular headless CMS, Contentful offers extensive API support and a user-friendly interface for content management, allowing teams to create and manage content efficiently across channels. Sanity : Known for its real-time collaboration features, Sanity allows teams to manage content dynamically. It also provides robust APIs that enable seamless integration with various front-end technologies. Storyblok : Known for its visual editor and flexibility, Storyblok allows content creators to design and manage content in a way that suits their needs. It offers robust API functionality, making it easy for developers to integrate it with various frontend frameworks. Why headless architecture is a must-have in omnichannel ecommerce Monolithic architectures, like for example Magento, are undoubtedly robust and offer a lot of useful features. However, its great power comes at a high cost when it comes to performance. Since they are one extra-large unit with a frontend tightly coupled to and dependent on the backend, monoliths can turn out to be very slow. The out-of-the-box features mean lots of code – and the more code you have, the longer it takes to process. With headless architecture, there is no need to render as much "default" code , making everything run faster. Headless commerce is a great choice for omnichannel expansion also because it gives brands the freedom to control each digital touchpoint independently. With frontend and backend layers decoupled, you can design unique user interfaces for different channels and update them quickly without altering the backend infrastructure. This flexibility is key for businesses aiming to deliver a unified customer experience, ensuring that users get consistent, high-quality interactions regardless of where they engage with the brand. But headless architecture is not only for enterprises Headless commerce is not limited to big global brands. This approach doesn't force a bloody revolution in the system by killing off the whole class of existing functionalities and restarting the architecture from the very beginning. On the contrary, headless commerce is very agile and enables the addition of new business functionalities to an existing monolithic architecture, and integrates with standard UI with almost no technical support. In practice, several different platforms (e.g., CRM, CMS, OMS, loyalty programs) can be ‘covered' under one umbrella (i.e., frontend). How can smaller businesses leverage headless architecture? By decoupling the frontend from backend systems, headless architecture enables marketing, content, and product teams to make updates independently without waiting on developer support. Smaller businesses can quickly adapt their customer-facing experiences, running promotions or adjusting content to meet demand with ease. Because headless architecture is so flexible, it empowers teams without deep technical knowledge to manage multiple channels, streamlining processes and reducing dependency on IT resources. For smaller businesses, this adaptability can be game-changing. It gives access to the same advanced capabilities that large enterprises use, including personalization, omnichannel reach, and real-time content updates. Conclusion: Is headless architecture the future? A headless approach to commerce allows users to develop systems at different speed: e.g. within the frontend with fast-paced design iteration and a field to explore new features, and within the backend with special attention to security and stability. For most companies looking to future-proof their digital infrastructure, headless architecture offers the flexibility and resilience required to stay relevant in a fast-paced ecommerce environment. Monoliths can still be effective for smaller companies with simple needs or limited technical resources, as they provide a single, cohesive system with out-of-the-box functionality. However, for businesses aiming to innovate quickly and scale efficiently, the monolithic approach falls short. Updating a monolithic system often requires lengthy development cycles and a full re-deployment, which can slow down a company's response to market changes and customer demands. So, is headless architecture the future? For businesses with ambitions to scale, adapt, and deliver exceptional customer experiences, the answer is a resounding yes.
